title: Shopping, money and numbers to 100
description: Ask prices, understand the answer, bargain and pay, using the numbers from eleven to a hundred.

guide.title: Eleven to sixteen
guide.text:
Bengali numbers up to a hundred are not built by a simple rule like 'twenty-one, twenty-two': each one is a single word that has to be learnt. The good news is that the pattern is visible once you know the units and the tens, and that everyone understands you if you say the digits one by one.

The numbers from eleven to eighteen all end in a spoken -o, now usually written with ো.

guide.title: Seventeen to thirty
guide.text:
Nineteen is 'one less than twenty': উনিশ. The same উন- prefix gives 29 (উনত্রিশ), 39 (উনচল্লিশ) and so on.

Twenty is কুড়ি (kuri) in West Bengal and বিশ (bish) in Bangladesh; both are understood everywhere. The twenties are built on the older form: একুশ (ekush) 21, বাইশ (baaish) 22, তেইশ (teish) 23, চব্বিশ (chobbish) 24, পঁচিশ (ponchish) 25.

Thirty is তিরিশ in everyday speech, ত্রিশ (trish) in writing.

guide.title: The tens
guide.text:
With the tens you can understand most prices, because shopkeepers round to five or ten.

ষাট (sixty) and সাত (seven) are both romanised shaat: sixty has the retroflex t (tongue curled back), seven the dental t (tongue on the teeth).

A hundred is একশো (eksho), also written একশ. Then দুশো (dusho) 200, তিনশো 300, পাঁচশো 500; হাজার (haajaar) 1,000; লাখ (laakh) 100,000.

guide.title: Hundreds, and the 'half' words
guide.text:
The currency is the টাকা (taakaa): the rupee in India, the taka in Bangladesh. The word also simply means 'money'. The amount comes first: পঞ্চাশ টাকা, 'fifty rupees'.

Bengali has special words for one and a half and two and a half, and they are used all the time with money, weights and clock times:

দেড় (der) one and a half - দেড়শো 150, দেড় কিলো 1.5 kg
আড়াই (aaraai) two and a half - আড়াইশো 250
সাড়ে (shaare) 'plus a half', from three and a half upwards - সাড়ে তিনশো 350, সাড়ে পাঁচ কিলো 5.5 kg

Never say সাড়ে এক or সাড়ে দুই.

guide.title: Asking the price and bargaining
guide.text:
দাম (daam) is 'price'. এটার দাম কত? 'What is the price of this?' - or just point and say কত? For things sold by weight: কত করে? (koto kore) 'how much each / per kilo?'

In markets and small shops without fixed prices, bargaining is expected and good-humoured. The standard moves: এত দাম! 'so much!'; একটু কম করুন, 'reduce it a little'; then name your figure with দেব, 'I'll give': দেড়শো টাকা দেব।

To close: ঠিক আছে, দিন - 'all right, give it to me'. To walk away politely: আমার লাগবে না - 'I won't need it'. To look without pressure: আমি শুধু দেখছি।

খুচরো (khuchro) is small change; ফেরত (pherot) is the change you get back.

examples.english: Please reduce the price a little.
I'll give a hundred and fifty rupees.

phrases.note: টাকা is the rupee in India and the taka in Bangladesh.

phrases.english: Please reduce the price a little.
I'll give a hundred and fifty rupees.

phrases.note: Literally 'I won't need it' - a polite way to refuse.

phrases.english: Do you have a bigger size?

phrases.note: You will hear this from shopkeepers too.
